extracted.intended_audience: European patent attorneys, patent applicants and EPO practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal standards about whether and how to amend the description of a European patent application prior to grant so that it is consistent with the allowed claims, including recent Boards of Appeal case law (T 1989/18 and T 1444/20) and relevant EPC provisions/guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidelines 2021 deletion requirement for embodiments not covered by independent claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2021 update of the Guidelines for Examination required that embodiments “in the description which are no longer covered by the independent claims must be deleted … unless these embodiments can reasonably be considered to be useful for highlighting specific aspects of the amended claims”, and further that in such case “the fact that an embodiment is not covered by the claims must be prominently stated”.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This represents an extremely strict approach introduced in 2021 that made minimal amendments insufficient in many cases; the text should be treated as a formal standard applicants and examiners relied on during prosecution. The guidance implies deletion of embodiments not covered by the claims unless they clearly serve to highlight aspects of the amended claims, and if retained they must be prominently labelled as not covered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board of Appeal T 1989/18 — no legal basis for general requirement to streamline description
rubrics_metrics.description: BoA 3.3.04 found there is no legal basis for the requirement that the description should be streamlined with the claims, and set aside a refusal based solely on the description identifying embodiments as part of the invention that were not part of the invention as defined by the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board examined possible legal bases (Art. 84, Art. 69 EPC, R.42(1)(c), R.48(1)(c)) and rejected them as justifying a general obligation to remove unclaimed subject-matter from the description. Practical takeaway: where claims are clear and supported by the description, the mere presence of additional embodiments in the description does not automatically justify refusal under Art.84 EPC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 84 EPC — scope and limitations regarding description amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: Art. 84 EPC requires claims to be clear and to be supported by the description; however, subject-matter in the description that does not appear in the claims is not prohibited and does not necessarily affect clarity of the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BoA reasoning: clarity of claims is the central requirement; additional unclaimed material in the description does not per se render claims unclear. When assessing whether amendments to the description are required, focus on whether the extra description impairs understanding of the technical problem/solution or clarity/support of the claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 69 EPC and Rules 42(1)(c), 48(1)(c) EPC are not a general justification for deleting description matter
rubrics_metrics.description: BoA held Art.69 EPC is irrelevant to amendments to the description because it concerns claim construction rather than defining the subject-matter for protection. R.42(1)(c) EPC was found satisfied if passages do not impair understanding of the technical problem and solution. R.48(1)(c) EPC aims to prevent publication of matter contrary to morality/public order and cannot be used to require removal of 'unnecessary information'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When arguing against examiner objections to description content, practitioners can rely on these limitations in using Art.69, R.42(1)(c) and R.48(1)(c) as legal bases for compulsory deletion; stress whether the contested passages actually impair understanding or offend public order/morality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim-like clauses in the description need not be deleted if they do not affect claim clarity (T 1444/20)
rubrics_metrics.description: BoA 3.3.01 in T 1444/20 held there is no reason why the presence of the section 'Specific embodiments of the invention' or 'claim-like clauses' should affect the clarity of the claims; numbered embodiments cannot be mistaken for claims since they are evidently part of the description and not denoted as 'claims'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board criticized the Guidelines for requiring mandatory removal of claim-like clauses while simultaneously acknowledging they may or may not cause a lack of clarity. Practical implication: do not delete claim-like fallback language from the description automatically — deletion is only justified if the clauses actually result in lack of clarity of the claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid labelling an embodiment as 'not covered by the claims' — deletion preferred to prevent carving a 'hole' in protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Labelling an embodiment as “not covered by the claims” might carve a “hole” into the scope of protection, the extent of which is difficult to foresee. It may provide a basis to argue that the claimed invention is a selection from described alternatives, with consequences under national law (e.g., German doctrine of equivalents / decision X ZR 76/14).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: prominently stating an embodiment is not covered by the claims. Better practice: fully delete such an embodiment from the description if the embodiment is not to fall within the scope. If retained, be aware of possible limiting consequences in infringement proceedings, especially in jurisdictions applying selection-from-alternatives reasoning that may exclude unclaimed alternatives as equivalents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior minimal amendment practice (pre-2021) and limited wording options
rubrics_metrics.description: Before 2021, it was often sufficient to supplement the description with statements such as “the invention is defined by the claims” to avoid extensive edits; the 2021 Guidelines made this approach less likely to be sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When considering how much to change the description before grant, note historical practices but do not assume they still carry weight. Use minimal clarifying statements cautiously and consider recent case law and examiners' likely expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical prosecution strategy — think twice before last-minute amendments and minimise limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: It is paramount for applicants to think twice before light‑heartedly making last‑minute amendments to the description at the end of prosecution, which may lead to a reduced scope of protection. Applicants should take utmost care to adapt the description in a manner that minimises any corresponding limitation of scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical tips: avoid unnecessary or overbroad deletions or labels that narrow scope; if a change is required, draft it to minimise unintended narrowing; consider implications under national infringement doctrines (e.g. doctrine of equivalents); when in doubt, challenge examiner requests relying on BoA reasoning (T 1989/18, T 1444/20) while factoring in likely examiner adherence to other decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate precedential weight and likely examiner treatment (distribution codes and subsequent decisions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The two decisions T 1989/18 and T 1444/20 were given the lowest distribution code 'D' (not distributed to other Boards), whereas other decisions (e.g. T 1024/18, T 2766/17, T 2293/18) that follow the standard EPO line were given distribution code 'C' (distributed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical consequence: despite favorable BoA rulings, examiners may continue to insist on extensive adaptations of the description. Practitioners should assess the likely treatment by the Examining Division and weigh the risk of arguing against deletion versus making carefully crafted edits to minimise limitation.
